items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “money owed by a country’s government, firms and people to foreign lenders”.

items.stem: Explain the causes of the debt crisis of the 1980s.
items.answer: Banks recycled petrodollars as cheap loans in the 1970s; oil price rises increased import bills; interest rates rose sharply in 1979-81; commodity prices fell; loans were spent on unproductive projects or lost to corruption; currencies fell.

items.stem: Explain the consequences of high debt for an LIC.
items.answer: Debt repayments divert money from health, education and infrastructure; austerity under SAPs; reduced investment; pressure to export commodities; reliance on new loans; social unrest.

Debt service ratio = debt service ÷ exports × 100; above 20% is often considered unsustainable. Explain why the debt service ratio is a useful measure of the burden of debt.
items.answer: Debt is repaid in foreign currency, mainly earned from exports, so the ratio shows the share of foreign earnings used for repayments rather than imports or investment.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that the causes of international debt lie mainly outside the indebted countries. In your answer you may refer to governance and lenders.
items.answer: For: Oil shocks, rising world interest rates, falling commodity prices, irresponsible lending by banks and later bond markets; strong dollar. Against: Domestic factors: corruption, poor investment choices, weak tax systems, conflict, excessive borrowing by governments; some countries with similar shocks avoided crisis. Conclusion: External shocks usually trigger debt crises, but domestic policies decide how vulnerable countries are.

options: The repayments of capital and interest on debt in a year.
Debt service as a percentage of export earnings; above about 20% is often regarded as unsustainable.
Money owed by a country’s government, firms and people to foreign lenders.
Conditions imposed by the IMF and World Bank in the 1980s-90s, such as cutting public spending and privatising industries, in return for loans.

items.stem: Compare bilateral and multilateral aid.
items.answer: Bilateral aid is given directly between governments and may reflect donors’ political and commercial interests, sometimes tied; multilateral aid is pooled through international agencies, less political, often for large programmes but may carry conditions.

items.stem: Explain the advantages of NGO aid.
items.answer: Small-scale, bottom-up projects using appropriate technology; works directly with communities; can reach the poorest; responsive in emergencies; less affected by corruption.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that aid does more to benefit donor countries than recipient countries. In your answer you may refer to health, governance and dependency.

items.answer: Money saved on repayments can be spent on health, education and infrastructure; improves credit ratings; reduces pressure to export commodities; encourages investment.

items.stem: Explain why debt relief has not solved the debt problem.
items.answer: Conditions delayed relief; only some debts were cancelled; countries borrowed again from new lenders at higher rates; commodity price falls and shocks; COVID-19.

items.stem: Hana argues that debt relief is more effective than aid in promoting development. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: Relief frees government budgets for long-term spending chosen by the country (Uganda, Tanzania abolished school fees); no administrative costs; reduces dependency. Against: Aid can target specific needs and the poorest (vaccines, water projects, emergencies); relief benefits governments that may be corrupt; many countries have new debts. Conclusion: Both are valuable; debt relief gives flexibility, while well-targeted aid addresses specific problems; governance determines the effectiveness of each.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the causes of international debt lie mainly outside the indebted countries?
items.answer: For: Oil shocks, rising world interest rates, falling commodity prices, irresponsible lending by banks and later bond markets; strong dollar. Against: Domestic factors: corruption, poor investment choices, weak tax systems, conflict, excessive borrowing by governments; some countries with similar shocks avoided crisis. Conclusion: External shocks usually trigger debt crises, but domestic policies decide how vulnerable countries are.
